title: Bread and Butter Pudding
subtitle: Classic baked bread pudding with custard, currants, and nutmeg
excerpt: Thick slices of buttered bread layered in a dish, covered with a spiced vanilla custard, scattered with currants, and baked until puffed and golden on top with a trembling, creamy interior.

recipe.sourceNotes: Bread and butter pudding is one of the oldest British puddings, appearing in cookbooks from the eighteenth century as a practical means of using stale bread. The basic form, bread soaked in a sweetened egg custard and baked, has barely changed: it is a pudding made from pantry staples when other resources run low. The dish experienced a revival in British restaurant cooking from the 1980s onwards, with versions using croissants, pain au chocolat, or brioche in place of plain bread. The classic home version uses white bread with crusts on, buttered generously. Raisins, currants, or sultanas are added between the layers. The custard is a standard vanilla baked custard: the proportions should give a softly set, creamy interior rather than a firm, rubbery texture. The pudding is best eaten warm from the oven, with pouring cream or a jug of creme anglaise alongside.

recipeTools.notes: A buttered baking dish, approximately 30 x 20 cm and 6 cm deep.

content.text: Leave the assembled pudding to soak for at least 30 minutes before baking: the bread needs time to absorb the custard fully. If the custard is poured over and baked immediately, the top layer of bread remains dry and the interior does not set evenly. Day-old bread absorbs more readily than very fresh bread. Serve the pudding within 20 minutes of it coming out of the oven: it deflates as it cools.

items.preparation: thick-cut, crusts on; slightly stale is better
softened, for spreading, plus extra for the dish

content.text: Butter the bread slices on one side. Butter a baking dish. Layer the bread slices in overlapping rows, buttered side up, scattering currants between the layers and leaving some on top.
Whisk the cream, milk, eggs, caster sugar, and vanilla together. Pour slowly and evenly over the bread. Grate nutmeg over the top. Leave to soak for 30 minutes to 1 hour.
Heat the oven to 170 C / fan 150 C / gas 3. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the custard is just set and the top is golden and beginning to caramelise. Dust with icing sugar and serve warm with cream.
